metadata.title: CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) OSCE
metadata.subtitle: 15 Structured Stations
metadata.audienceAndScoring: Final-Year MBBS • 8 minutes per station • 20-point analytic checklist
metadata.includedMaterials: Candidate materials • Standardised scripts • Examiner guides • Learning notes
facultyNote: This manual follows the same station architecture as the preceding OSCE manuals. Patient names in source scenarios have been changed. Stations 1–4 are anchored directly in the supplied CNS notes; additional stations are selected to cover high-yield final-year KMU Neurosciences-III psychomotor/OSCE objectives and CPSP-style focused clinical assessment, interpretation, differential diagnosis and management planning. Safety note: the supplied notes contain some older prescribing/referral statements. Exact drug doses, thrombolysis criteria, antithrombotic timing, imaging pathways, seizure rescue treatment and infection management must be checked against current approved institutional/provincial/national protocols before summative use.
assessmentDesign: Each analytic checklist totals 20 points: 10 criteria scored 0–2.
Prompted performance scores a maximum of 1/2 for that item.
A critical safety error may justify an overall fail despite the numeric score.
contents: 2. First Adult Seizure — History & Safety Counselling
4. TIA / Acute Stroke — FAST & Focused Assessment
6. CT Brain — Epidural vs Subdural Haematoma
7. CT Brain — Ischaemic vs Intracerebral Haemorrhage
11. Lower Limb Neurology / Myotomes in GBS

stations.title: Migraine — Focused History & Management
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused neurological history, differential diagnosis and management
candidateInstructions: Take a focused history of this patient with recurrent severe headache. Explain the likely diagnosis and outline initial management.
candidateHandout: Clarify time course before labelling a headache.
Screen for meningitis, SAH, raised ICP, trauma and focal neurology.
For migraine ask aura, unilateral pulsatile pain, nausea, photophobia/phonophobia and triggers.
simulationScript: Mr Ahsan Raza, 34-year-old office worker.
Right-sided throbbing headache for 2 days, 7/10, nausea, photophobia and phonophobia.
Visual zig-zag aura precedes headache. Better lying in a dark quiet room.
Similar attack 6 months ago; father has similar headaches.
No fever, neck stiffness, trauma, persistent focal deficit or thunderclap onset.
Concern: “Could this be a brain tumour?”
examinerInstructions: Do not volunteer red flags unless asked.
Award management credit for evidence-based acute treatment and safety-netting rather than memorised drug doses.
keyAnswerGuide: Most likely migraine with aura.
Red flags requiring urgent evaluation include thunderclap onset, meningism/fever, altered consciousness, focal deficit, papilloedema/raised ICP features and significant trauma.
Management: explanation, trigger diary, sleep/meals/hydration, acute simple analgesic/NSAID ± antiemetic; triptan when appropriate; preventive therapy if frequent/disabling after assessment.
suggestedApproach: Address concern, explain diagnosis and agree management.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, confirms patient and consent.
Defines onset, duration, site, character and severity.
Asks nausea/vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia.
Asks aura and functional impact.
Screens fever/neck stiffness and altered consciousness.
Screens thunderclap onset, trauma and focal neurology.
Asks previous episodes, drugs and family history.
Explores triggers and medication overuse.
Explains likely migraine and acute/preventive options.
Safety-nets urgent red flags and arranges follow-up.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: What features favour migraine?
Name three secondary-headache red flags.
criticalSafetyErrors: Reassures without screening red flags.
Misses sudden thunderclap headache or focal neurological deficit.
sourceNote: Source-derived: supplied CNS notes — headache classification and migraine scenario. Management modernised for safe teaching use.

stations.title: First Adult Seizure — History & Safety Counselling
stations.primaryCompetency: Seizure history, differential diagnosis and counselling
candidateInstructions: Take a focused history of a possible first seizure and counsel the patient about immediate safety and next steps.
candidateHandout: An eyewitness description is often crucial.
Ask prodrome/aura, ictal features and post-ictal state.
Screen provoking factors and mimics.
simulationScript: Ms Zoya Khan, 27-year-old teacher, seen after a first unprovoked collapse with shaking.
Witness saw sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening then bilateral jerking for ~90 seconds.
Lateral tongue bite and post-event confusion for 20 minutes. No preceding chest pain/palpitations.
Sleep deprived recently; no alcohol/drug withdrawal.
No previous seizure. No current focal deficit.
examinerInstructions: Candidate should advise urgent specialist assessment for first suspected seizure and appropriate investigations.
Do not reward a specific antiseizure drug choice as mandatory in a first-seizure station.
keyAnswerGuide: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure is likely.
History: injury, CNS infection, stroke, febrile seizures, family history, substances/withdrawal, sleep deprivation, flashing lights; medication review.
Assess glucose and basic labs; ECG where syncope is a differential; specialist-directed EEG/neuroimaging.
Safety: avoid driving until medically cleared under applicable law, heights, unsupervised swimming/bathing, open flames/machinery.
suggestedApproach: Identify provoked vs unprovoked seizure and mimics.
Check immediate safety and arrange specialist pathway.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self and confirms event chronology.
Obtains eyewitness features and duration.
Asks aura/prodrome and loss of awareness.
Asks tongue bite/incontinence/injury.
Assesses post-ictal confusion/Todd weakness.
Screens syncope and metabolic/toxic precipitants.
Asks neurological history, drugs/substances and family history.
Proposes glucose/basic tests, ECG and specialist EEG/imaging as appropriate.
Provides seizure first-aid and personal safety advice.
Arranges urgent specialist review and clear return precautions.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: What features distinguish seizure from syncope?
What advice follows a first suspected seizure?
criticalSafetyErrors: Allows driving or hazardous activity without restriction pending assessment.
Fails to consider hypoglycaemia or ongoing neurological deficit.
sourceNote: Source-derived: supplied CNS notes — adult epilepsy/first seizure history and referral principles; wording updated for current safe assessment.

stations.title: Febrile Seizure — Parent Counselling
stations.primaryCompetency: Paediatric seizure history and parent counselling
candidateInstructions: Take a focused history from the parent and explain the likely diagnosis, first aid and red flags.
candidateHandout: A simple febrile seizure is typically brief, generalised and followed by recovery.
Always screen for meningitis/serious infection and complex seizure features.
simulationScript: Mrs Mahnoor Ali, mother of 18-month-old Rayyan, who had a fever-associated convulsion.
Rayyan had fever 39.4°C and a generalised convulsion lasting 3 minutes, then slept and returned to baseline.
First episode. No focal features or recurrence within 24 hours.
No non-blanching rash, persistent drowsiness or neck stiffness. Immunisations up to date.
Mother asks if he now has epilepsy.
examinerInstructions: Assess whether candidate identifies simple vs complex features.
Credit calm first-aid counselling; do not require outdated routine cooling measures.
keyAnswerGuide: Likely simple febrile seizure if age/context and examination fit.
First aid: protect from injury, place on side when possible, do not restrain or put objects in mouth, time the seizure, seek emergency help for prolonged seizure or concerning features.
Treat child discomfort/fever appropriately and assess source of fever; antipyretics do not reliably prevent recurrence.
suggestedApproach: Address parental concern and teach seizure first aid.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self and confirms child details.
Clarifies seizure description, duration and recovery.
Asks fever and likely infection symptoms.
Screens focality, recurrence and prolonged seizure.
Screens meningism, non-blanching rash and persistent altered state.
Reviews development, immunisation and previous/family seizures.
Explains likely febrile seizure in understandable language.
Demonstrates correct seizure first aid.
Explains when emergency care is required.
Arranges assessment/follow-up for fever source and parental concerns.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: What makes a febrile seizure complex?
What should a parent do during another seizure?
criticalSafetyErrors: Advises restraining the child or placing an object in the mouth.
Misses meningitis red flags or prolonged seizure.
sourceNote: Source-derived: supplied CNS notes — febrile fits scenario. First-aid wording updated to contemporary safety practice.

stations.title: TIA / Acute Stroke — FAST & Focused Assessment
stations.primaryCompetency: Acute stroke recognition, FAST/NIHSS-oriented assessment and emergency action
candidateInstructions: Assess this patient with sudden focal neurological symptoms. Demonstrate FAST and state your immediate priorities.
candidateHandout: Treat ongoing focal deficit as stroke until proven otherwise.
Record last-known-well time and activate emergency stroke pathway.
FAST is a rapid screen; NIHSS is a structured severity assessment.
simulationScript: Mr Sameer Hussain, 66, sudden left arm and face weakness 35 minutes ago.
Symptoms began suddenly 35 minutes ago while eating breakfast.
Left facial droop and left arm weakness; speech is slurred.
Hypertension and diabetes; no recent trauma.
No seizure at onset.
examinerInstructions: Provide simulated findings when candidate performs FAST.
Candidate must not delay emergency transfer for a lengthy clinic work-up.
keyAnswerGuide: FAST: facial asymmetry, arm drift/weakness, speech disturbance, time/last known well.
Immediate priorities: ABC, capillary glucose, vitals, focused neuro assessment, urgent brain imaging and stroke-team pathway.
Do not give antithrombotic treatment blindly before the acute stroke pathway has excluded haemorrhage and considered reperfusion eligibility.
suggestedApproach: Perform FAST and focused neurological assessment.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self and assesses ABC/overall stability.
Establishes exact onset/last-known-well.
Checks facial asymmetry.
Assesses arm power/drift bilaterally.
Assesses speech/language.
Checks capillary glucose and vital signs.
Screens anticoagulants, bleeding risk, seizure/trauma and baseline function.
States urgent non-contrast CT/appropriate imaging.
Activates stroke/emergency pathway and considers reperfusion assessment.
Communicates urgency and avoids unsafe delay/treatment.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: What does FAST stand for?
Why is last-known-well time critical?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delays emergency transfer.
Gives empiric antithrombotic therapy without appropriate acute stroke assessment/imaging.
sourceNote: Source-derived: supplied TIA/stroke material plus KMU Neurosciences-III emphasis on FAST/NIHSS and acute stroke assessment.

stations.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
candidateInstructions: Demonstrate and calculate the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) on this patient. State the score and immediate implication.
candidateHandout: Score Eye (4), Verbal (5), Motor (6) separately.
Use the best observed response and document components, not only the total.
simulationScript: Mr Daniyal Shah, 52, reduced consciousness after a road traffic collision.
Simulation findings are supplied by examiner.
examinerInstructions: E: opens eyes to speech = 3. V: confused conversation = 4. M: localises pain = 5. Total 12/15.
Ensure ABC/cervical-spine precautions in trauma.
keyAnswerGuide: Trend serial GCS; deterioration is clinically important.
suggestedApproach: Assess safely, then eye, verbal and motor response.
Relate to urgency and repeat assessment.

checklist.criterion: Checks immediate safety/ABC and trauma precautions.
Assesses spontaneous eye opening then appropriate stimulus.
Scores eye response correctly.
Assesses verbal response appropriately.
Scores verbal response correctly.
Assesses motor response using command then stimulus if needed.
Scores motor response correctly.
States E3 V4 M5 and total 12/15.
Mentions serial reassessment and pupil/vital monitoring.
Escalates deterioration/reduced consciousness appropriately.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: Why document E/V/M separately?
What other observations accompany GCS?
criticalSafetyErrors: Uses unsafe painful stimulus technique.
Fails to address airway risk in a deteriorating patient.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: directly aligned with KMU Neurosciences-III psychomotor objective for GCS assessment.

stations.title: CT Brain — Epidural vs Subdural Haematoma
candidateInstructions: Interpret the two non-contrast CT brain images and distinguish epidural from subdural haematoma. State one urgent management principle for each.
candidateHandout: Epidural: classically biconvex/lentiform extra-axial collection.
Subdural: classically crescentic extra-axial collection.
Assess mass effect, midline shift and clinical deterioration.
simulationScript: CT images are provided for two head-injury patients: Ms Eman Noor, 22, and Mr Haris Khan, 71.
Image A: hyperdense biconvex collection after temporal trauma.
Image B: crescentic hyperdense collection over cerebral convexity after a fall.
examinerInstructions: Accept correct radiological pattern recognition and urgency.
keyAnswerGuide: A = acute epidural haematoma; B = acute subdural haematoma.
Both require ABC stabilization, urgent neurosurgical discussion and management guided by clinical/imaging severity.
suggestedApproach: Describe location, density, shape and mass effect.

checklist.criterion: Confirms non-contrast CT brain.
Uses systematic image orientation.
Describes extra-axial hyperdensity in A.
Recognises biconvex/lentiform morphology.
Diagnoses epidural haematoma.
Describes crescentic extra-axial hyperdensity in B.
Diagnoses subdural haematoma.
Comments on mass effect/midline shift.
States urgent ABC/neurosurgical escalation.
Relates imaging to clinical deterioration/GCS.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: Which collection is classically lentiform?
What imaging feature makes this immediately dangerous?
criticalSafetyErrors: Fails to recognise intracranial haemorrhage as an emergency.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: KMU specifically lists CT identification of epidural and subdural haematoma.

stations.title: CT Brain — Ischaemic vs Intracerebral Haemorrhage
candidateInstructions: Interpret the CT brain images in the context of acute stroke and state how the distinction affects immediate treatment.
candidateHandout: Non-contrast CT is used urgently to identify haemorrhage and guide acute stroke decisions.
Early ischaemic CT can be normal or show subtle changes.
simulationScript: Two CT images: Mr Taimoor Aziz, 64, acute aphasia; Ms Alina Javed, 59, sudden hemiplegia and vomiting.
Image A: no acute haemorrhage; subtle early ischaemic change.
Image B: focal hyperdense intraparenchymal collection with surrounding mass effect.
examinerInstructions: Do not require advanced radiology grading.
keyAnswerGuide: A: likely acute ischaemic stroke after haemorrhage excluded; assess reperfusion eligibility.
B: intracerebral haemorrhage; no thrombolysis; urgent BP/anticoagulation/neurosurgical or stroke-team management per protocol.
suggestedApproach: Describe findings, integrate with clinical presentation, state immediate pathway.

checklist.criterion: Confirms non-contrast CT brain.
Checks for haemorrhage systematically.
Recognises absence of haemorrhage in A.
Identifies possible early ischaemic changes in A.
Links A to reperfusion eligibility assessment.
Recognises intraparenchymal hyperdensity in B.
Diagnoses intracerebral haemorrhage.
States thrombolysis is contraindicated in haemorrhage.
Mentions urgent specialist stroke/neurosurgical management.
Communicates limitations and need for clinical correlation.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: Can an early ischaemic CT be normal?
Why must haemorrhage be excluded urgently?
criticalSafetyErrors: Recommends thrombolysis for intracerebral haemorrhage.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: KMU Neurosciences-III requires interpretation of CT/MRI in stroke and recognition of haemorrhagic stroke.

stations.title: Meningitis — Lumbar Puncture on Mannequin
stations.primaryCompetency: Lumbar puncture technique and meningitis safety
candidateInstructions: Demonstrate the steps of lumbar puncture on the mannequin. You do not need to insert a real needle. State key contraindications and specimen handling.
candidateHandout: Use aseptic technique and correct lumbar level.
Assess for contraindications/need for imaging before LP; do not delay life-saving treatment in suspected bacterial meningitis when LP is unsafe or delayed.
simulationScript: Mr Shahzaib Iqbal, 24, fever, headache and neck stiffness; mannequin provided.
Mannequin, sterile tray and labelled specimen tubes are provided.
examinerInstructions: Expect consent, positioning, landmarking, asepsis, local anaesthetic, needle direction, CSF collection, aftercare.
keyAnswerGuide: Typical level L3/4 or L4/5 using iliac-crest line as landmark.
CSF studies depend on scenario: cell count, protein, glucose with paired blood glucose, microbiology/culture ± other tests.

checklist.criterion: Confirms identity, indication, consent and allergies.
Checks contraindications/raised ICP concerns, coagulopathy and cardiorespiratory stability.
Positions lateral decubitus or seated appropriately.
Identifies L3/4 or L4/5 landmark.
Performs hand hygiene, sterile preparation and draping.
Describes local anaesthetic and sterile spinal needle technique.
Directs needle correctly and recognises CSF return.
Collects sequential labelled tubes appropriately.
Requests appropriate CSF/blood studies.
Applies dressing, monitors patient and documents/escalates complications.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: When should LP be deferred?
Which CSF tests are important in suspected meningitis?
criticalSafetyErrors: Performs LP despite clear contraindication/instability.
Uses non-sterile technique.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: KMU explicitly lists lumbar puncture technique for CNS/spinal infections (meningitis).

stations.title: Cranial Nerve Examination
candidateInstructions: Perform a focused cranial nerve examination. Present your findings and localise the likely lesion.
candidateHandout: Be systematic and compare sides.
Include pupils/eye movements, facial motor/sensory function and bulbar function as clinically appropriate.
simulationScript: Ms Iqra Salman, 41, diplopia and facial asymmetry.
Examiner supplies findings: right abduction weakness; otherwise normal.
examinerInstructions: Candidate should identify right VI nerve palsy if examination is performed correctly.
keyAnswerGuide: Right lateral rectus weakness = right abducens (VI) palsy.
Consider raised ICP, microvascular, cavernous sinus/brainstem and other causes depending context.
suggestedApproach: Inspect, visual pathways/pupils, ocular movements, face, hearing, palate/voice, shoulder/tongue as appropriate.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, consent and checks visual symptoms.
Assesses visual acuity/fields appropriately.
Examines pupils and light responses.
Tests ocular movements and asks about diplopia/nystagmus.
Assesses facial sensation and corneal reflex conceptually when indicated.
Tests facial movements.
Assesses hearing grossly.
Assesses palate/voice/swallow-related CN function safely.
Tests shoulder shrug/head turn and tongue.
Summarises right VI palsy and proposes localisation/differentials.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: Which muscle abducts the eye?
Give causes of an isolated VI palsy.
criticalSafetyErrors: Misses new diplopia with neurological red flags or unsafe swallow assessment.
sourceNote: Added CPSP-style focused short-case station: systematic examination, correct findings, localisation and differential diagnosis.

stations.title: Upper Limb Neurological Examination
candidateInstructions: Perform a complete neurological examination of both upper limbs and present your findings.
candidateHandout: Sequence: inspection → tone → power → reflexes → coordination → sensation.
Use MRC power grading and compare sides.
simulationScript: Mr Affan Malik, 58, right-hand weakness after a neurological event.
Findings: increased tone right arm, pyramidal weakness, brisk reflexes, reduced fine movement; sensory exam normal.
examinerInstructions: Provide findings only when manoeuvre is correctly performed.
keyAnswerGuide: Pattern suggests upper motor neuron lesion affecting right upper limb.
Localise with other signs/context rather than naming a cause from the limb exam alone.
suggestedApproach: Inspect, tone, power, reflexes, coordination, sensation.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, consent and adequate exposure.
Inspects for posture, wasting, fasciculation and involuntary movement.
Assesses tone correctly.
Tests major myotomes/muscle groups with MRC grading.
Tests biceps, supinator and triceps reflexes.
Assesses finger-nose and rapid alternating movements.
Tests light touch/pinprick in relevant distribution.
Assesses proprioception/cortical sensation when indicated.
Compares sides and identifies UMN pattern.
Presents findings clearly and suggests localisation/next exam.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: How do UMN and LMN signs differ?
Which reflexes assess C5–C7?
criticalSafetyErrors: Causes pain/injury by excessive force.
Calls an UMN pattern peripheral neuropathy without reconciliation.
sourceNote: Added high-yield CPSP-style neurological short case focused on systematic examination and localisation.

stations.title: Lower Limb Neurology / Myotomes in GBS
stations.primaryCompetency: Lower limb neurological examination, myotomes and GBS recognition
candidateInstructions: Perform a focused lower-limb neurological examination with emphasis on myotomes and reflexes. State the likely syndrome and immediate safety concern.
candidateHandout: GBS classically causes progressive symmetrical weakness with reduced/absent reflexes.
Respiratory and autonomic involvement can be life-threatening.
simulationScript: Ms Anaya Rahman, 32, progressive ascending leg weakness after diarrhoeal illness.
Findings: symmetrical proximal/distal weakness, absent knee/ankle jerks, plantar flexor responses, mild distal paraesthesia.
examinerInstructions: If candidate recognises GBS, ask what must be monitored urgently.
keyAnswerGuide: Likely Guillain–Barré syndrome.
Urgent hospital assessment; monitor respiratory function and autonomic instability; evaluate for mimics and specialist treatment.
suggestedApproach: Assess gait if safe, tone, power by myotome, reflexes, plantars and sensation.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, consent and checks safety before gait.
Inspects and assesses tone.
Tests hip flexion L1/2 and knee extension L3/4.
Tests ankle dorsiflexion L4/5 and great-toe extension L5.
Tests plantarflexion S1.
Tests knee and ankle reflexes.
Assesses plantar responses.
Checks sensation and symmetry.
Recognises ascending areflexic weakness compatible with GBS.
States urgent respiratory/autonomic monitoring and specialist admission.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: Which myotome tests great-toe extension?
What makes GBS immediately dangerous?
criticalSafetyErrors: Fails to assess/mention respiratory compromise.
Encourages unsafe ambulation in marked weakness.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: KMU specifically lists practical performance of myotomes in Guillain–Barré syndrome.

stations.title: Cerebellar Examination
candidateInstructions: Perform a focused cerebellar examination and present your findings.
candidateHandout: Assess speech, eyes/nystagmus, upper-limb coordination, lower-limb coordination and gait when safe.
Differentiate cerebellar ataxia from sensory ataxia.
simulationScript: Mr Rameez Akhtar, 49, unsteady gait and clumsiness.
Findings: scanning dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus, right dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, broad-based gait.
examinerInstructions: Provide findings with correct manoeuvres.
keyAnswerGuide: Right-sided appendicular cerebellar signs with gait ataxia.
Complete neuro exam and investigate acute vs chronic cause.
suggestedApproach: Gait/tandem gait if safe; Romberg as a sensory comparison rather than a primary cerebellar test.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, consent and assesses fall risk.
Assesses speech.
Checks eye movements/nystagmus.
Performs finger-nose accurately.
Tests dysdiadochokinesia.
Tests rebound appropriately/safely or explains.
Performs heel-shin test.
Assesses gait and broad base.
Attempts tandem gait only if safe and interprets Romberg appropriately.
Summarises laterality and suggests completion/localisation.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: What is dysdiadochokinesia?
How does sensory ataxia differ?
criticalSafetyErrors: Allows a markedly ataxic patient to walk unsupported.
sourceNote: Added high-yield CPSP-style neurological short case assessing focused examination, findings and localisation.

stations.title: Parkinsonism — Focused Examination
candidateInstructions: Examine this patient for parkinsonism and present the key positive findings.
candidateHandout: Core parkinsonism: bradykinesia plus rigidity and/or rest tremor; assess gait/postural features.
Look for atypical/red-flag features.
simulationScript: Mr Waleed Farooq, 68, slowness and tremor.
Findings: hypomimia, 4–6 Hz right rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, reduced right arm swing, short shuffling steps.
examinerInstructions: Do not force pull test if unsafe.
keyAnswerGuide: Findings support parkinsonism, clinically compatible with Parkinson disease if no atypical features.
Assess medications, cognition, autonomic symptoms, falls and functional impact.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, consent and observes facial expression/posture.
Characterises rest tremor.
Assesses tone/rigidity with activation if needed.
Tests finger tapping for bradykinesia.
Tests hand opening/closing or pronation-supination.
Assesses lower-limb bradykinesia.
Assesses rising from chair safely.
Observes gait, stride and arm swing.
Assesses postural stability only when safe.
Summarises parkinsonism and mentions medication/atypical-feature review.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: Define bradykinesia clinically.
Name two atypical features that should prompt reconsideration.
criticalSafetyErrors: Performs unsafe pull test without guarding.
sourceNote: Added high-yield CPSP-style short case: focused examination and interpretation of a common neurological syndrome.

stations.title: Spinal Cord Compression — Recognition & Immobilisation
stations.primaryCompetency: Spinal cord compression recognition and spinal immobilisation
candidateInstructions: Recognise the neurological emergency and demonstrate safe initial spinal immobilisation/handling principles.
candidateHandout: Red flags: severe spinal pain, bilateral weakness/sensory change, sphincter dysfunction, saddle symptoms, cancer/infection/trauma context.
Avoid unnecessary movement; maintain alignment and urgent specialist pathway.
simulationScript: Ms Hania Siddiqui, 45, severe back pain, bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention after metastatic cancer treatment.
Progressive bilateral leg weakness over 24 hours, numbness to lower trunk, urinary retention.
Known breast cancer.
examinerInstructions: Candidate should identify cord compression and urgent MRI/specialist escalation.
Use available collar/board only as appropriate to scenario and local trauma protocol.
keyAnswerGuide: Suspected metastatic spinal cord compression.
Immediate neurological assessment, urgent MRI of appropriate spine and urgent specialist oncology/neurosurgery/spinal pathway; immobilise if instability/trauma suspected.
suggestedApproach: Assess neurological level and sphincter symptoms.
Protect spine when instability is possible.

checklist.criterion: Recognises spinal cord compression as emergency.
Asks onset/progression and severe spinal pain.
Assesses bilateral motor deficit.
Assesses sensory level/saddle symptoms.
Asks bladder/bowel dysfunction.
Identifies cancer/infection/trauma risk factors.
Maintains spinal alignment and minimises unsafe movement.
Demonstrates appropriate collar/immobilisation principles if indicated.
Requests urgent MRI and specialist pathway.
Communicates urgency and documents serial neurology.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: What features suggest cord rather than root disease?
When is spinal immobilisation particularly important?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delays imaging/referral despite sphincter dysfunction and progressive weakness.
Moves a potentially unstable spine unsafely.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: KMU lists spinal cord compression/syndromes and demonstration of proper spine immobilisation with collars.

stations.title: Status Epilepticus — Emergency Management
candidateInstructions: Demonstrate your immediate management priorities for an ongoing convulsive seizure and explain the escalation plan if it continues.
candidateHandout: Use an ABCDE approach and time the seizure.
Correct hypoglycaemia and other reversible causes.
Follow current local status-epilepticus protocol for rescue and second-line medication.
simulationScript: Mr Azlan Qureshi, 36, ongoing generalised convulsive seizure in the emergency department.
Generalised convulsions have continued for >5 minutes. Oxygen saturation is falling. Capillary glucose result is available on request.
examinerInstructions: Reward prioritisation over memorised doses.
Exact medication/dose must follow the institution’s current emergency protocol.
keyAnswerGuide: Convulsive status epilepticus is a medical emergency.

Protect from injury, airway/oxygen/suction as needed, monitoring, IV/IO access, glucose, labs, first-line benzodiazepine per protocol, then second-line antiseizure therapy and anaesthetic/ICU escalation if refractory.
Search for cause: non-adherence, metabolic disturbance, infection, stroke, toxin/withdrawal, pregnancy-related causes where relevant.
suggestedApproach: Investigate cause and escalate refractory seizure.

checklist.criterion: Calls for senior/emergency help and times seizure.
Protects patient from injury; does not restrain or place objects in mouth.
Manages airway, oxygenation and suction appropriately.
Attaches monitoring and obtains IV/IO access.
Checks capillary glucose and treats hypoglycaemia if present.
States first-line benzodiazepine per current protocol.
States timely second-line antiseizure therapy if ongoing.
Plans ICU/anaesthetic escalation for refractory status.
Requests appropriate labs/imaging/infection work-up after stabilisation.
Communicates and documents seizure duration, drugs and response.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring rule: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/incorrect/unsafe.
promptQuestions: When does a convulsive seizure become status epilepticus for emergency treatment purposes?
What reversible causes must be checked immediately?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delays airway/glucose assessment while taking a long history.
Restrains the patient or puts an object in the mouth.
Repeats sedating medication without monitoring/escalation.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station: KMU Neurosciences-III includes diagnostic work-up/management of fits, tonic-clonic epilepsy and status epilepticus; CPSP viva assesses emergency problem-solving.
